idiom_name: @AroundInvoke interceptor methods bound by annotations, dispatched by the container
implementation_notes: The container owns the dispatcher: an interceptor class carries a method annotated @AroundInvoke that receives an InvocationContext, may inspect or replace parameters, and must call ctx.proceed() to continue the chain and reach the target method - not calling it vetoes the business method. Attachment is declarative: an interceptor binding annotation on the target class or method selects which interceptors apply, so the target code stays untouched, and ordering is controlled by @Priority or the @Interceptors order. The classic Interceptor/Dispatcher class pair is replaced by the container plus annotations; a hand-written chain is still justified off-container (plain unit tests, unmanaged objects), where the JDK dynamic proxy form is used instead. Spring's HandlerInterceptor (preHandle/postHandle/afterCompletion) is the same idea for HTTP handlers rather than bean methods.
pitfalls: Self-invocation bypasses everything: a business method calling another method on the same instance does not pass through the proxy, so the interceptors silently do not run.
Ordering is only guaranteed with explicit @Priority (or an ordered @Interceptors list); otherwise the container decides, and a security interceptor can end up after the code it was meant to guard.
Interceptors are container-managed and effectively shared, so request state in instance fields leaks across concurrent invocations - use InvocationContext.getContextData() or call-scoped beans.
Interception applies to business methods of managed beans: final, static and private methods, and beans constructed with new, are invisible to it.

variants.name: java.lang.reflect.Proxy over interface methods
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK-level mechanism the containers use underneath: Proxy.newProxyInstance builds a class implementing the given interfaces at run time and dispatches every interface method call to an InvocationHandler, whose invoke(proxy, method, args) receives the Method object as the event name and the arguments as the context. Attachment is per instance - hand out the proxy instead of the target - so an interceptor can be added or removed for one collaborator without touching the framework, at the cost that only calls made through the proxy are intercepted. Choose this when no container is available or when the interception must be wired explicitly; prefer the container form when annotations and lifecycle management are acceptable.
pitfalls: Exceptions from method.invoke arrive wrapped in InvocationTargetException - unwrap getCause() or the caller's catch blocks stop matching.
Only interface methods are intercepted; hashCode/equals/toString are routed too, so a careless handler breaks collection behaviour.
Proxy classes end up in the package of the proxied interfaces (or a dynamic module for non-exported ones), which can surprise code relying on getClass()/reflection.
Calls to the target object made directly (not through the proxy) bypass the handler entirely, and each proxy instance needs its own handler state.
